currency pair.definition: Two currencies quoted against each other, like EUR/USD. The price is how much of the second currency one unit of the first costs.

base currency.definition: The first currency in a pair. In EUR/USD it's the euro.

quote currency.definition: The second currency in a pair, the one the price is measured in. In EUR/USD it's the US dollar.

broker.definition: The company that holds your account and fills your orders. Check that it's regulated before you deposit anything.

pip.definition: The standard small price step. The fourth decimal place for most pairs (0.0001), the second for yen pairs (0.01).

lot.definition: A unit of trade size. A standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency, a mini lot 10,000 and a micro lot 1,000.

leverage.definition: Controlling a position bigger than your deposit. It makes gains and losses larger in money terms; it doesn't change the odds.

margin.definition: The part of your balance a broker sets aside to keep a leveraged position open.

spread.definition: The gap between the buy and sell price. You pay it on every trade.

stop-loss.definition: An order that closes a trade at a set price to cap the loss. It may fill worse than its price in fast markets or over gaps.

position size.definition: How big a trade is, in lots. It sets how much money each pip is worth.

r-multiple.definition: A trade's result divided by the money risked on it. Risk $10 and make $25: +2.5R.

expectancy.definition: The average result per trade, in R, across many trades. Shown with its range, because small samples mislead.

win rate.definition: Winning trades divided by closed trades. On its own it says nothing about whether a strategy makes money.

drawdown.definition: The fall from an account's highest point to its lowest point after it, as a percentage or in R.

liquidity.definition: How easily something can be bought or sold without moving its price. More buyers and sellers means more liquidity.

volatility.definition: How much and how fast a price moves. High volatility means bigger, quicker swings.

slippage.definition: The difference between the price you asked for and the price your order actually filled at.

swap.definition: The overnight financing charge or credit for holding a position past the daily rollover, based on the two currencies’ interest rates.

gap.definition: A jump in price between one quote and the next, with no trading in between, often after a weekend or big news.

margin call.definition: A warning from your broker that your equity is close to the level needed to keep positions open.

stop-out.definition: When a broker automatically closes your positions because your margin has fallen to its minimum level.

negative balance protection.definition: A rule or broker policy that stops a retail account from falling below zero, so you can’t owe more than you deposited.

session.definition: The trading hours of a major financial centre, such as Asia, London or New York.

support.definition: A price area where falling prices have stopped before, because buyers stepped in.

resistance.definition: A price area where rising prices have stopped before, because sellers stepped in.

trend.definition: A sustained direction in price: higher highs and higher lows (uptrend) or lower highs and lower lows (downtrend).

candlestick.definition: A chart bar showing a period’s open, high, low and close prices.

moving average.definition: The average closing price over a set number of recent periods, redrawn as each new period closes.

rsi.definition: Relative Strength Index: an indicator from 0 to 100 that compares recent gains with recent losses.

atr.definition: Average True Range: the average size of a period’s full price range, used to measure volatility.

timeframe.definition: The period each bar or candle on a chart covers, such as 15 minutes, 4 hours or 1 day.

interest rate.definition: The cost of borrowing money, or the return for lending it, as a percentage per year.

central bank.definition: The institution that sets a country’s main interest rate and manages its currency, such as the Federal Reserve or the Central Bank of Nigeria.

inflation.definition: The rate at which prices in an economy rise over time.

carry trade.definition: Holding a higher-interest currency against a lower-interest one to earn the difference, while taking on exchange rate risk.

correlation.definition: How closely two prices tend to move together, from +1 (same direction) to −1 (opposite directions).

edge.definition: A repeatable advantage: rules whose results, after costs, have shown a positive expectancy on data they weren’t built on.

backtest.definition: Testing a strategy’s rules on past price data to see how they would have performed.

overfitting.definition: Tuning a strategy so closely to past data that it fits the noise, not a real pattern, and then fails on new data.

out-of-sample.definition: Data a strategy wasn’t built or tuned on, kept aside to test it fairly.

sample size.definition: How many trades or observations a result is based on. Small samples can show almost anything by chance.

mechanical strategy.definition: A strategy whose rules are precise enough that two people would take exactly the same trades.

discretionary strategy.definition: A strategy that leaves some decisions to the trader’s judgement in the moment.

risk of ruin.definition: The chance that losses shrink an account to a level you can’t or won’t recover from.

profit factor.definition: Total winning R divided by total losing R. Above 1 means the wins outweighed the losses.

equity curve.definition: A chart of an account’s value, or cumulative R, trade by trade over time.

confidence range.definition: The range a true value probably lies in, given the data. Fewer trades means a wider range.

tilt.definition: Trading driven by emotion after losses or frustration, usually outside the rules.

trading journal.definition: A record of every trade with its reasons, rule checks, result and how you felt.

prop firm.definition: A company that sells trading challenges and offers to share profits on a funded account if you pass its rules.
